images.text: We all know that tension and worry often affect us physically. Some people even report that they feel ill due to strain and pressure. (Who has not written at least one test in school that made them sick?) Doctors warn that those who are tense and worried over a long period of time may well develop real illnesses. The mind affects the body. Conversely, when we feel relaxed, our bodies simply feel better. Consider singing. Have you ever sung in the shower with no one around to see you or hear you? It is not difficult to let loose freely with a song. Now imagine you have just been asked to sing on a stage in front of people. Most of us will admit that we become quite nervous and tense in front of people. Some will even report that butterflies are too much to bear, and that they cannot sing at all.

One reputable drama teacher states that yawning is a great way to battle nerves. She says that when you yawn and stretch, your body naturally relaxes itself. All you have to do is seriously start pretending to yawn, and then your body will take over and you will really start yawning! Some people brush this technique off as being wacky and unproven, but she always asks the doubters what they have to lose. She tells them that the worst that can happen is that they feel a little sleepy.

Another wonderful way to relax is by laughing. Some doctors recommend it as a deliberate exercise to be done every day. Again, start laughing by just doing it, and then the body will naturally take over. Knowing how to relax is important. Modern performers have been very aware of this. In order to become fit, they have begun paying attention to stress management. If you've been backstage at a race or a show recently, you have certainly seen an artist or two laughing and yawning. They're not tired or giggly, they're just trying to reduce their anxiety. I guess they are  just trying to fake it ‘till they make it!

Present Perfect: Present Results of Past Action
You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.
Have you ever sung in the shower with no one around to see or hear you?
Now imagine you have just been asked to sing on a stage in front of people.
Modern performers have become very aware of this.
If you've been backstage at a race or a show recently, you have certainly seen an artist or two laughing and yawning.

You use that- clauses and wh- clauses to report statements and questions in indirect speech.

You use reported speech to report statements or situations.
You use that- clauses to report someone else's thoughts or statements.
Example:
Jo suggested that I should go exercise more.

You use wh- clauses to report questions with wh- words like why, when, what, who, etc.
With wh- clauses, you normally use verbs like ask, want to know, wonder to introduce the clause.
Example:
Jo asked me when I was going to exercise next.
